intro: Walk into a Buddhist temple and you may see shelves of books, bundles of palm leaves or long scrolls. These are Buddhist scriptures. There are so many that people call them a library, not one book.

In this unit you will learn how the oldest collection, the Tipitaka, is sorted into three baskets. You will see where the Dhammapada and the Jatakas fit. You will also learn about the Mahayana sutras kept in Chinese and Tibetan.

Then you will follow the teachings on their long trip. They went from memory and chanting to palm leaves, printed scrolls and English books. By the end, you will be able to explain how the Buddhist library is built and how it traveled.
bigQuestion: What are the Buddhist scriptures, and how did they reach us?

timeline.t: The Buddha teaches in northern India (dates vary; many scholars say the 5th century BCE).
Tradition says the First Council meets at Rajagaha soon after the Buddha's death (dates vary).
In King Ashoka's time, Buddhism reaches Sri Lanka.
Tradition says monks write the Pali Canon on palm leaves at Aluvihara.
Buddhist texts begin to reach China.
Kumarajiva translates many sutras into Chinese.
Tibetan scholars begin large translation projects.
The Diamond Sutra is block printed in China.
Muller's Dhammapada appears; Rhys Davids founds the Pali Text Society.
Buddhist speakers address the World's Parliament of Religions in Chicago.
The Dunhuang library cave is found in China.
The Buddhist Temple of Chicago is founded.

title: What the Buddhist Texts Are

chapters.title: The Three Baskets
chapters.bigQuestion: How are the Buddhist scriptures organized, and why is there no single Buddhist Bible?

story.title: Three Baskets on a Shelf
story.kicker: A monk explains why the old books were once stored in three baskets.
paragraphs: A fourth-grade class visits a Theravada Buddhist temple near Chicago. A monk in an orange robe greets them at the door. He bows slightly with his palms together. The students bow back.
He leads them to a wooden shelf. On it sit rows of books with gold letters. "These are our scriptures," he says. "We call them the Tipitaka. That means three baskets."

A boy named Omar raises his hand. "Why baskets?" The monk smiles. "Long ago, in India, workers passed dirt and bricks along in baskets. Some teachers say the name came from that. Others say the palm-leaf books were kept in baskets. Either way, the teachings were sorted into three groups."
He holds up three fingers. "One basket is for rules for monks and nuns. One is for the Buddha's talks. One is for careful lists about the mind." The students count along with him.
Omar looks at the long shelf. "That is a lot of books," he says. The monk nods. "And this is only one part of the Buddhist library." The students look around the room with new eyes.
story.think: Why might a big collection of teachings be sorted into groups?

lessons.title: Three Baskets in Pali
lessons.mainIdea: The Tipitaka, or three baskets, is the collection of scriptures Theravada Buddhists use, written in the Pali language.
reading: Theravada Buddhists in Sri Lanka, Thailand, Myanmar, Cambodia and Laos share one big set of scriptures. It is called the *Tipitaka*. The word means "three baskets." Tipitaka is the Pali form. The Sanskrit form is Tripitaka.

The Tipitaka is written in *Pali*. Pali is an old language from India. Few people speak it at home today. Monks learn it to read and chant the texts. English readers often call this collection the Pali Canon.

Buddhists believe the Tipitaka holds the Buddha's teachings as his students remembered them. Scholars say it grew over several centuries. Both groups agree it is very old and very large. The English translation fills dozens of books.

words.d: "three baskets"; the collection of scriptures in the Pali language
an old language of India used for Theravada Buddhist scriptures

look.title: The Three Baskets
look.unit: basket number, in the usual order
look.cite: The Pali Tipitaka, Pali Text Society editions (1877 onward)

check.q: What does Tipitaka mean?
check.why: Tipitaka is a Pali word meaning three baskets.

check.q: What language is the Tipitaka written in?
check.why: The Theravada scriptures are in Pali, an old language of India.

check.q: Which Buddhists use the Pali Tipitaka as their main scripture?
check.why: Theravada Buddhists in countries like Thailand and Sri Lanka use the Pali Canon.

lessons.title: The Vinaya Basket
lessons.mainIdea: The Vinaya holds the rules for Buddhist monks and nuns and stories of why each rule was made.
reading: The first basket is the *Vinaya*. It holds the rules for monks and nuns. The rules cover eating, clothing, sleeping and living together. They also explain how to settle arguments.

Each rule comes with a story. The Vinaya tells what happened, and then how the Buddha made a rule about it. For example, it tells of monks traveling in the rainy season. Farmers worried about their crops being stepped on. So monks were asked to stay in one place during the rains.
Theravada monks recite the main list of rules together twice a month. This list is called the *Patimokkha*. For fully ordained monks it has 227 rules. Nuns have a longer list.

words.d: the basket of rules for Buddhist monks and nuns
the main list of monastic rules, recited twice a month

look.title: A Rule With a Story
look.text: A class makes a rule: "Push in your chair." Why? Last week someone tripped over one. The Vinaya works the same way. Each rule comes with the story of what happened first.
look.prompt: Why might it help to know the story behind a rule?

check.q: What is in the Vinaya?
check.why: The Vinaya is the basket of monastic rules.

check.q: How many rules are on the Theravada monks' main list?
check.why: The Theravada Patimokkha for monks has 227 rules. 423 is the number of Dhammapada verses.

check.q: Why do monks stay in one place during the rains, says the Vinaya?
choices: so they would not trample crops
check.why: The Vinaya says farmers worried about crops, so monks stayed put in the rainy season.

lessons.title: The Sutta and Abhidhamma Baskets
lessons.mainIdea: The Sutta basket holds the Buddha's talks, and the Abhidhamma basket holds careful lists about the mind.
reading: The second basket is the Sutta basket. A *sutta* is a talk or teaching. The Sanskrit word is sutra. Most suttas show the Buddha or a student teaching someone. There are thousands of them.
The suttas are grouped into five collections called Nikayas. Some hold long talks. Some hold middle-length talks. One, the Khuddaka Nikaya, holds a mix of shorter books.

The third basket is the *Abhidhamma*. It sorts ideas about the mind into careful lists. It names kinds of thoughts and feelings. Theravada teachers value it highly. Many scholars think it was put together later than the suttas.

words.d: a talk or teaching of the Buddha (Sanskrit: sutra)
the basket of careful lists and explanations about the mind

look.prompt: Which collection has the fewest suttas? Why might that be?

check.q: What is a sutta?
check.why: A sutta is a talk or teaching, usually by the Buddha or a student.

check.q: What is the Abhidhamma about?
check.why: The Abhidhamma sorts ideas about the mind into lists.

check.q: What is the Sanskrit form of sutta?
check.why: Sutta is the Pali form and sutra the Sanskrit form.

lessons.title: The Dhammapada
lessons.mainIdea: The Dhammapada is a short book of 423 verses inside the Sutta basket.
reading: The *Dhammapada* sits in the Khuddaka Nikaya, the collection of shorter books. Its name means something like "path of the teaching." It has 423 short verses in 26 chapters.
Many Buddhists memorize its verses. They are short and easy to remember, like proverbs. Chapters have names like "The Mind," "Flowers" and "Anger." Readers often quote them.
The Dhammapada is one of the best-known Buddhist books in the world. It has been translated into many languages. One of the first English translations was by F. Max Muller in 1881.

words.d: a book of 423 short verses in the Pali Canon
a short numbered piece of a sacred text

look.title: The Dhammapada's First Verse
look.text: All that we are is the result of what we have thought: it is founded on our thoughts, it is made up of our thoughts.
look.cite: Dhammapada 1, tr. F. Max Muller, Sacred Books of the East vol. 10 (1881)
look.prompt: In your own words, what does this verse say comes first?

check.q: How many verses are in the Dhammapada?
check.why: The Dhammapada has 423 verses. It has 26 chapters.

check.q: Which basket holds the Dhammapada?
check.why: The Dhammapada is in the Khuddaka Nikaya of the Sutta basket.

check.q: Who made an early English translation in 1881?
check.why: F. Max Muller translated the Dhammapada in 1881.

lessons.title: The Jatakas
lessons.mainIdea: The Jatakas, stories of the Buddha's earlier lives, are also in the Sutta basket.
reading: The Khuddaka Nikaya also holds the *Jatakas*. These are stories Buddhists tell about the Buddha's earlier lives. There are about 547 of them. The stories are often long.
In the Pali Canon itself, each Jataka is a set of verses. A later commentary tells the full story around the verses. Most people know the stories from that commentary.
The last ten Jatakas are long and famous. The very last is the story of Prince Vessantara, who gives away everything he has. Buddhists in Thailand and Laos still hear it told at festivals.

words.d: a story of one of the Buddha's earlier lives
a later book that explains an older text

look.title: Verses and Story
look.text: In the canon, the Hare Jataka is a few short verses. The commentary adds the four friends, the traveler and the moon. The verses are the heart. The story is the body around it.
look.prompt: Why might a teacher add a story around a few verses?

check.q: About how many Jatakas are there?
check.why: The Pali collection has about 547 Jatakas.

check.q: What is a commentary?
choices: a later book that explains an older text
check.why: A commentary explains an older text. The Jataka stories come mostly from one.

check.q: Who is the hero of the last Jataka?
check.why: The last Jataka tells of Prince Vessantara's giving.

lessons.title: "Thus Have I Heard"
lessons.mainIdea: Suttas usually begin "Thus have I heard," words tradition gives to the Buddha's student Ananda.
reading: Many suttas begin the same way: "Thus have I heard." In Pali it is *evam me sutam*. Then the sutta names a place. It might say the Buddha was staying in a park near a city.
Buddhist tradition says the "I" is Ananda. He was the Buddha's cousin and helper. He was known for his memory. Tradition says he recited the suttas after the Buddha died.
The opening tells listeners where a teaching came from. It says, in effect, "I did not make this up. I heard it." Mahayana sutras start the same way. It also marks the start.

words.d: the Buddha's cousin and helper, remembered for his memory
Pali for "Thus have I heard," the usual opening of a sutta

look.title: How a Sutta Opens
look.text: Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was staying near a city, in a park given by a friend.
look.cite: The standard opening of Pali suttas (e.g., Digha Nikaya 16), paraphrased
look.prompt: What two things does this opening tell the listener?

check.q: How do many suttas begin?
check.why: Suttas usually open with "Thus have I heard," evam me sutam.

check.q: Who does tradition say the "I" is?
check.why: Buddhist tradition says Ananda recited the suttas.

check.q: Why does the opening matter?
choices: it tells where the teaching came from
check.why: The opening says the speaker heard the teaching, not made it up.

lessons.title: Mahayana Sutras
lessons.mainIdea: Mahayana Buddhists also treasure many other sutras, first written in Sanskrit and kept in Chinese and Tibetan.
reading: *Mahayana* Buddhism is followed in China, Japan, Korea, Vietnam and Tibet. Mahayana means "great vehicle." Mahayana Buddhists honor many early texts too. They also treasure many other sutras.

Famous ones include the Lotus Sutra, the Heart Sutra and the Diamond Sutra. Many were first written in Sanskrit. Many Sanskrit copies were later lost. They survive in Chinese and Tibetan translations.
Mahayana Buddhists believe these sutras teach the Buddha's deepest message. Scholars date most of them from about the 1st century BCE onward. Theravada Buddhists do not include them in their canon.

words.d: "great vehicle"; the branch of Buddhism common in East Asia and Tibet
a famous Mahayana sutra, much loved in China and Japan

check.why: Mahayana means great vehicle.

check.q: Which is a Mahayana sutra?

check.q: Where do many Mahayana sutras survive?
check.why: Many Sanskrit originals were lost, but Chinese and Tibetan translations survive.

lessons.title: No Single Buddhist Bible
lessons.mainIdea: Buddhism has no one book that every Buddhist uses; different traditions keep different collections.
reading: Some religions have one main book. Buddhism is different. Buddhists have a large library of scriptures. Different traditions choose different parts. The library is very big.
A Theravada monk in Thailand reads the Pali Canon. A Zen teacher in Japan may chant the Heart Sutra. A Tibetan nun studies texts in the Kangyur. Each is reading Buddhist scripture.
Many families also have favorite texts. A Pure Land Buddhist may love a sutra about Amitabha Buddha. A Nichiren Buddhist chants the name of the Lotus Sutra. No one book holds it all.

words.d: a writing a religion treats as sacred
a branch or way of practice passed down over time

check.why: A scripture is a writing a religion treats as sacred.

lessons.title: Where the Branches Live
lessons.mainIdea: Theravada, Mahayana and Vajrayana Buddhism grew strong in different parts of Asia and now live in America too.
reading: Theravada Buddhism is strongest in Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia. Mahayana Buddhism grew in China, Korea, Japan and Vietnam. *Vajrayana* Buddhism is strongest in Tibet, Bhutan and Mongolia.
Each branch has its own favorite scriptures. Each has its own ways of practice. Buddhists in each branch see themselves as following the Buddha. None is ranked above the others here.
All three branches are found in Illinois today. Families from Thailand, Japan, Vietnam, Tibet and many other places have temples here. The Buddhist Temple of Chicago was founded in 1944.

words.d: "way of the elders"; the branch of Buddhism using the Pali Canon
"diamond vehicle"; the branch of Buddhism common in Tibet and Mongolia

check.why: Theravada is strongest in Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia.

check.why: The Buddhist Temple of Chicago was founded in 1944.

review.why: The Vinaya holds the monastic rules.

chapters.title: From Memory to Palm Leaves
chapters.bigQuestion: How did the Buddha's teachings travel from spoken words to the books we have today?

story.title: Five Hundred in a Cave
story.kicker: Five hundred monks sit in a cave, and one of them begins, "Thus have I heard."
paragraphs: Buddhist tradition tells this story. A few months after the Buddha died, his students gathered near the city of Rajagaha. They met in a large cave in the hills. Five hundred senior monks came.
They had a big worry. The Buddha had taught for many years. But he had written nothing down. How would they keep his words safe? Some of the monks looked at one another in silence.
First a monk named Upali stood. He recited the rules for monks and nuns. The others listened closely. When he finished, they agreed that his words were correct.
Then Ananda stood. He had been the Buddha's helper for many years. He had heard more teachings than anyone. The cave was quiet. Ananda began: "Thus have I heard."
The monks chanted the teachings back together. Buddhists call this meeting the First Council. For hundreds of years after, the teachings lived in memory and chanting.
story.think: Why might a group chanting together help keep words from changing?

lessons.title: The First Council
lessons.mainIdea: Tradition says the Buddha's students met after his death to recite and agree on his teachings.
reading: Buddhist tradition says a meeting was held soon after the Buddha died. It is called the First *Council*. A council is a meeting to decide something important. Tradition places it at Rajagaha, in northern India.
The Vinaya tells the story. It says 500 monks attended. Upali recited the rules. Ananda recited the talks. The group agreed on what they heard. Then they chanted it together.
Scholars cannot check every detail of this story. Many think the texts grew and changed over time. Buddhists and scholars both agree the teachings were first passed on by voice, not writing.

words.d: a meeting to decide something important
to say something aloud from memory

look.title: Early Councils, as Tradition Tells
rows: First Council, soon after the Buddha's death
Third Council, time of King Ashoka, c. 250 BCE
look.cite: Cullavagga 11–12 (Vinaya); Sri Lankan chronicles, Dipavamsa and Mahavamsa
look.prompt: About how long after the first council was the second, as tradition tells it?

check.q: Who recited the rules at the First Council?
check.why: Tradition says Upali recited the Vinaya and Ananda the suttas.

check.q: What is a council?
choices: a meeting to decide something important
check.why: A council is a meeting to decide something important.

check.q: What do Buddhists and scholars agree on?
choices: the texts were written at once
the teachings were first passed on by voice
check.why: Both agree the teachings began as spoken words, even if they differ on details.

lessons.title: Ananda's Memory
lessons.mainIdea: Tradition remembers Ananda as the monk with the best memory, who recited the suttas.
reading: *Ananda* was the Buddha's cousin. For about 25 years he was the Buddha's personal helper. He walked beside him and brought him water. He heard many talks.
Buddhists remember Ananda for his memory. Tradition says he could repeat a teaching after hearing it once. That is why the council asked him to recite.
Ananda is also remembered for his kindness. The Vinaya says he spoke up for women who wanted to become nuns. Many Buddhists honor him for that today. Nuns still tell this story.

words.d: the Buddha's cousin and helper, remembered for his memory
the ability to keep and recall what you learned

look.title: A Helper Who Listened
look.text: Picture a monk walking one step behind his teacher every day for years. He carries a water pot. He listens to every talk. At night he repeats the words to himself.
look.prompt: Why would a helper like this be good at remembering?

check.q: How was Ananda related to the Buddha?
check.why: Tradition says Ananda was the Buddha's cousin.

check.q: What is Ananda remembered for?
check.why: Ananda is remembered for his memory of the Buddha's talks.

check.q: Who did Ananda speak up for, says the Vinaya?
choices: women who wanted to be nuns
check.why: The Vinaya says Ananda asked the Buddha to let women become nuns.

lessons.title: Chanting Together
lessons.mainIdea: For centuries, monks kept the teachings by chanting them together.
reading: After the council, groups of monks memorized different parts of the texts. They chanted them together, again and again. This is called oral *tradition*.
Chanting together helps catch mistakes. If one monk says a word wrong, the others notice. Repeated lists and phrases made the texts easier to remember.
Scholars say the suttas show signs of this. They repeat whole lines many times. They use numbered lists, like the Four Noble Truths. These help memory.

words.d: teachings passed on by speaking and memory, not writing
to say or sing words together in a steady rhythm

look.title: Why Repeat?
look.text: A song has a chorus that comes back again and again. Soon you know it by heart. The suttas often repeat whole lines, too. A student hears the pattern and remembers.
look.prompt: What songs or rhymes do you know by heart? Why do you remember them?

check.q: What is oral tradition?
choices: passing on teachings by speaking and memory
check.why: Oral tradition passes teachings on by voice and memory.

check.q: How does chanting together help?
check.why: When a group chants, a wrong word gets noticed.

check.q: What helped monks remember the suttas?
check.why: Scholars point to repetition and lists as memory aids.

lessons.title: Palm Leaves in Sri Lanka
lessons.mainIdea: Tradition records that the Pali Canon was first written down on palm leaves in Sri Lanka in the 1st century BCE.
reading: Buddhism reached Sri Lanka around the 3rd century BCE. Monks there kept chanting the texts. Then came hard times, with war and famine. Many monks died.
The Sri Lankan chronicles say monks worried the teachings might be lost. So they wrote them down. Tradition places this at Aluvihara in the 1st century BCE.
They wrote on *palm leaves*. Writers scratched letters into dried leaves with a metal pen. Then they rubbed in ink or soot to make the letters dark. The leaves were tied into bundles.

words.d: a dried leaf used as a page for writing in South and Southeast Asia
a history book that lists events in order

look.title: From Voice to Book
rows: The Buddha teaches (scholars: c. 5th century BCE)
Canon written at Aluvihara (c. 1st century BCE)
look.prompt: About how many years passed between the Buddha's teaching and the writing down?

check.q: Where was the Pali Canon first written down, says tradition?
check.why: The Sri Lankan chronicles place it at Aluvihara in Sri Lanka.

check.q: Why did monks write it down, say the chronicles?
choices: they feared the teachings might be lost
check.why: War and famine made monks fear the teachings could be lost.

check.q: What did the writers use?
check.why: They scratched letters into dried palm leaves.

lessons.title: Making a Palm-Leaf Book
lessons.mainIdea: Palm-leaf books were made by hand, and copies had to be made again and again.
reading: A palm-leaf book is long and thin. Each leaf has holes. A string runs through the holes. Wooden covers protect the pages. The covers are often painted or carved with care.
Palm leaves slowly wear out. Heat, bugs and damp harm them. So monks copied the texts onto new leaves every so often. Copying was careful, slow work. A copy could take months.
Many Buddhist temples in Sri Lanka, Thailand and Myanmar still keep palm-leaf books. Some libraries study them today. Very old leaves are rare, because most wore out.

words.d: a book written by hand
to write something again so there is another one

look.title: Holding a Palm-Leaf Book
look.text: Picture a bundle of long, narrow leaves, as wide as your hand. Tiny dark letters run across them. Two wooden boards hold the bundle. A string ties it closed.
look.prompt: What problems might a palm-leaf book have in a hot, wet place?

check.q: What is a manuscript?
check.why: A manuscript is a handwritten book.

check.q: Why did monks copy palm-leaf books?
check.why: Heat, bugs and damp harm palm leaves, so new copies were needed.

check.q: What holds a palm-leaf book together?
check.why: A string runs through holes in the leaves.

lessons.title: The Diamond Sutra of 868
lessons.mainIdea: A printed Diamond Sutra from 868 CE is the oldest dated printed book known.
reading: In 1900 a monk in Dunhuang, China, found a hidden cave room. It was full of old scrolls. One was a copy of the *Diamond Sutra*, a Mahayana text. The cave had been sealed for centuries.
It was printed with carved wooden blocks. At the end it gives a date that matches 868 CE. It says a man named Wang Jie had it made for his parents. It is the oldest dated printed book known.
Today it is kept at the British Library in London. The scroll is about 16 feet long. It shows how Buddhists in China used printing to share their texts.

words.d: a Mahayana sutra; a printed copy from 868 CE is the oldest dated printed book known
printing by pressing carved wooden blocks with ink onto paper

look.title: Old Books, Old Dates
look.cite: British Library, Or.8210/P.2; common dates for the Gutenberg Bible
look.prompt: About how many years older is the Diamond Sutra than the Gutenberg Bible?

check.q: What year is printed on the Dunhuang Diamond Sutra?
check.why: Its date matches 868 CE, the oldest dated printed book known.

check.q: How was it printed?
check.why: It was made by block printing.

check.q: Where is it kept today?
check.why: The Diamond Sutra scroll is at the British Library in London.

lessons.title: Into Chinese and Tibetan
lessons.mainIdea: Translators carried Buddhist texts into Chinese and Tibetan over many centuries.
reading: Buddhism reached China by about the 1st century CE. Translators worked for centuries to turn texts into Chinese. One famous translator was Kumarajiva, around 400 CE.
Buddhism reached Tibet in the 7th and 8th centuries CE. Tibetan scholars made careful *translations* from Sanskrit. They made word lists so each term was translated the same way.
Some texts now survive only in Chinese or Tibetan. Without these translators, many sutras would be lost. Buddhists in East Asia and Tibet read them in their own languages.

words.d: a text turned from one language into another

look.title: One Word, Many Languages
look.text: The Sanskrit word for the teaching is dharma. In Pali it is dhamma. In Chinese it is fa. In Tibetan it is cho. It is one idea carried in many words.
look.prompt: Why is translating a sacred word so hard?

check.q: Who was Kumarajiva?
check.why: Kumarajiva translated many sutras into Chinese around 400 CE.

check.q: What did Tibetan scholars make to help translate?
check.why: They made word lists so each term was translated the same way.

check.q: What is the Pali form of dharma?
check.why: Dharma is Sanskrit and dhamma is Pali.

lessons.title: Into English
lessons.mainIdea: Scholars began translating Buddhist texts into English in the 1800s, and Chicago hosted Buddhist speakers in 1893.
reading: In the 1800s, European scholars began to study Pali and Sanskrit. F. Max Muller translated the Dhammapada in 1881. T.W. Rhys Davids translated suttas that same year. He also founded the Pali Text Society in 1881.
In 1893 the World's *Parliament* of Religions met in Chicago. Two Buddhist speakers came. Anagarika Dharmapala came from Sri Lanka. Soyen Shaku, a Zen teacher, came from Japan.
Today many translations exist. Buddhist monks, nuns and scholars all translate. Some translations are free online. Readers can compare them side by side.

words.d: a large meeting of religious leaders held in Chicago in 1893

look.title: An 1881 Translation
look.text: For hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love, this is an old rule.
look.cite: Dhammapada 5, tr. F. Max Muller, Sacred Books of the East vol. 10 (1881)
look.prompt: What word did Muller choose for what ends hatred? Can you think of another word a translator might use?

check.q: Who founded the Pali Text Society in 1881?
check.why: T.W. Rhys Davids founded the Pali Text Society in 1881.

check.q: Where was the 1893 World's Parliament of Religions?
check.why: The Parliament met in Chicago in 1893.

check.q: Who came from Sri Lanka to speak in 1893?

review.why: Tradition says Ananda recited the suttas and Upali the rules.

review.q: How were the teachings kept before writing?
review.why: Monks kept them by oral tradition, memory and chanting.

review.q: Where was the Pali Canon first written down, says tradition?
review.why: The chronicles say it was written at Aluvihara in Sri Lanka.

review.q: What is special about the Dunhuang Diamond Sutra?

it is the first palm-leaf book

review.q: Why did monks keep copying palm-leaf books?
review.why: Palm leaves are harmed by heat, bugs and damp.
